scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.
Decoded footprints extend from approximately -72.467 to -71.128 longitude and 21.431 to 21.958 latitude in both 1783 and 1938. This supports shared island identity, not exact coastline accuracy.

The term Lucayan has been applied differently to later Turks and Caicos communities in specialist research. The card uses Lucayan and other Taino communities and avoids fixing an ethnic replacement date. Opening phases are approximate, not first arrival or depopulation endpoints.
The museum Lucayan page contains outdated evaluative and extinction language that is not adopted. Its colonial-disruption account does not establish that every descendant vanished.

Paddle dates are calibrated radiocarbon estimates; the wood-family identification remains tentative and is omitted. Conservation chemistry is described without copying speculative explanatory analogies. No vulnerable find coordinates are given.
The 2013 house article is by the museum chairman who describes the fieldwork. The museum replica has a modern structural core. Common observed house features are not universal household rules.

The water-project report was published in February 2014, as confirmed by UKOTCF annual report 2013-2014 and its retrospective in Forum News 46. It distinguishes an existing practice on Grand Turk from planned work on Providenciales. No claim is made that the latter had already been installed at the launch.

The museum salt page gives 1833 as emancipation and different museum pages give different final shipment dates. Neither simplification is used. No precise abolition phase is inferred from those statements.

Mary Prince’s first-person account, printed pages 10 to 12 in the 1831 book, is paraphrased separately from the editor’s supplementary material. No disputed exact dates of her salt labour are assigned.
The governmental culture page contains old demographic figures and unsupported medical efficacy claims. Only craft teaching, music and territorial identity are used.

Only the 1799, 1848, 1874 and 1962 administrative account is used from the museum-hosted Mills history; its simplified early French occupation claim is omitted. Parliament’s history has an apparent 1967/1976 transposition and inconsistent nineteenth-century dates; the selected 1962, 1976 and 1986 to 1988 passages avoid those errors.

The 2009 to 2012 account distinguishes the corruption investigation from criminal convictions and notes opposition to direct rule. A British parliamentary briefing is an institutional perspective, not everyone’s view.
The ending concerns continuing communities and territorial status, not a verified political succession edge. New text awaits independent review.

sharedAssociations.basis: Decoded 1783 and 1938 snapshots cover the same Turks and Caicos island groups, east of the Bahamian archipelago. A shared regional narrative explicitly distinguishes Indigenous communities and later colonial institutions.
